metadata.title: Information theory and hypothesis testing, in Lean

nodes.name: Risk
nodes.statement: The risk of an estimator $\hat{y}$ on the estimation problem $(P, y, \ell')$ at $\theta \in \Theta$ is $r^P_\theta(\hat{y}) = (\hat{y} \circ P)(\theta)\left[z \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right]$~.
nodes.label: def:risk

nodes.name: Bayesian risk
nodes.statement: The Bayesian risk of an estimator $\hat{y}$ on $(P, y, \ell')$ for a prior $\pi \in \mathcal M(\Theta)$ is $R^P_\pi(\hat{y}) = \pi\left[\theta \mapsto r^P_\theta(\hat{y})\right]$~. It can also be expanded as $R^P_\pi(\hat{y}) = (\pi \otimes (\hat{y} \circ P))\left[ (\theta, z) \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z) \right]$~.
nodes.label: def:bayesianRisk

nodes.name: Bayes risk
nodes.statement: The Bayes risk of $(P, y, \ell')$ for prior $\pi \in \mathcal M(\Theta)$ is $\mathcal R^P_\pi = \inf_{\hat{y} : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z} R^P_\pi(\hat{y})$~, where the infimum is over Markov kernels. The Bayes risk of $(P, y, \ell')$ is $\mathcal R^*_B = \sup_{\pi \in \mathcal P(\Theta)} \mathcal R^P_\pi \: .$
nodes.label: def:bayesRisk

nodes.name: Bayes estimator
nodes.statement: An estimator $\hat{y}$ is said to be a Bayes estimator for a prior $\pi \in \mathcal P(\Theta)$ if $R^P_\pi(\hat{y}) = \mathcal R^P_\pi$.
nodes.label: def:bayesEstimator

nodes.name: Minimax risk
nodes.statement: The minimax risk of $(P, y, \ell')$ is $\mathcal R^* = \inf_{\hat{y} : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z} \sup_{\theta \in \Theta} r^P_\theta(\hat{y})$~.
nodes.label: def:minimaxRisk

nodes.statement: $\mathcal R_B^* \le \mathcal R^*$.
nodes.label: lem:bayesRisk_le_minimaxRisk

nodes.statement: For any $\pi \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)$ and any estimator, $\pi\left[\hat{\mu}_\theta\left[\ell'(y(\theta), \hat{y}(\theta))\right]\right] \le \sup_{\theta \in \Theta}\hat{\mu}_\theta\left[\ell'(y(\theta), \hat{y}(\theta))\right]$.

The Bayes risk of a prior $\pi \in \mathcal M(\Theta)$ on $(P, y, \ell')$ with $P$ a Markov kernel satisfies \begin{align*} \mathcal R^P_\pi \le \inf_{z \in \mathcal Z} \pi\left[ \theta \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z) \right] \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:bayesRisk_le_const

nodes.statement: The infimum over all Markov kernels in the definition of the Bayes risk of $\pi$ is bounded from above by the infimum restricted to constant, deterministic Markov kernels.

The Bayes risk of a prior $\pi \in \mathcal M(\Theta)$ on $(P, y, \ell')$ with $P$ a constant Markov kernel is \begin{align*} \mathcal R^P_\pi = \inf_{z \in \mathcal Z} \pi\left[\theta \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right] \: . \end{align*} In particular, it does not depend on $P$.
nodes.label: lem:bayesRisk_const

nodes.statement: Let $\xi$ be the measure such that $P(\theta) = \xi$ for all $\theta$. \begin{align*} \mathcal R^P_\pi &= \inf_{\hat{y}}(\pi \times (\hat{y} \circ \xi))\left[(\theta, z)\mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right] \\ &= \inf_{\mu \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)} (\pi \times \mu)\left[(\theta, z)\mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right] \\ &= \inf_{\mu \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)} \mu\left[ z \mapsto \pi\left[\theta \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right]\right] \\ &= \inf_{z \in \mathcal Z} \pi\left[\theta \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right] \: . \end{align*}

nodes.name: Data-processing inequality
nodes.statement: For $P : \Theta \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$ and $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X'$ a Markov kernel, $\mathcal R^{\kappa \circ P}_\pi \ge \mathcal R^{P}_\pi$ (where the estimation problems differ only in the kernel).
nodes.label: thm:data_proc_bayesRisk

nodes.statement: The risk $\mathcal R^{\kappa \circ P}_\pi$ is \begin{align*} \mathcal R^{\kappa \circ P}_\pi &= \inf_{\hat{y} : \mathcal X' \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z} (\pi \otimes (\hat{y} \circ \kappa \circ P))\left[(\theta, z) \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right] \\ &\ge \inf_{\hat{y} : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z} (\pi \otimes (\hat{y} \circ P))\left[(\theta, z) \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right] \\ &= \mathcal R^{P}_\pi \: . \end{align*} The inequality is due to taking an infimum over a larger set: $\{\hat{y} \circ \kappa \mid \hat{y} : \mathcal X' \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z \text{ Markov}\} \subseteq \{\hat{y}' : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z \mid \hat{y} \text{ Markov}\}$~.
For $P : \Theta \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$ and $\kappa : \Theta \times \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X'$ a Markov kernel, $\mathcal R^{P \otimes \kappa}_\pi \le \mathcal R^{P}_\pi$~.
nodes.label: lem:bayesRisk_compProd_le_fst

nodes.statement: Use Theorem~\ref{thm:data_proc_bayesRisk}: $P$ is the composition of $P \otimes \kappa$ and the deterministic kernel $\mathcal X \times \mathcal X' \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$ that forgets the second value.

For $P : \Theta \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$ and $\kappa : \Theta \times \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X'$ a Markov kernel, $\mathcal R^{P \otimes \kappa}_\pi \le \mathcal R^{(P \otimes \kappa)_{\mathcal X'}}_\pi$~, in which $(P \otimes \kappa)_{\mathcal X'} : \mathcal \Theta \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X'$ is the kernel obtained by marginalizing over $\mathcal X$ in the output of $P \otimes \kappa$~.
nodes.label: lem:bayesRisk_compProd_le_snd

nodes.statement: Use Theorem~\ref{thm:data_proc_bayesRisk}: $(P \otimes \kappa)_{\mathcal X'}$ is the composition of $P \otimes \kappa$ and the deterministic kernel $\mathcal X \times \mathcal X' \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X'$ that forgets the first value.
The Bayes risk $\mathcal R_\pi^P$ is concave in $P : \Theta \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$~.
nodes.label: lem:bayesRisk_concave

nodes.statement: The infimum of a sum is larger than the sum of the infimums: \begin{align*} \mathcal R_\pi^{\lambda P_1 + (1 - \lambda)P_2} &= \inf_{\hat{y} : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z} (\pi \otimes (\hat{y} \circ (\lambda P_1 + (1 - \lambda)P_2)))\left[(\theta, z) \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right] \\ &= \inf_{\hat{y} : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z} \left( \lambda (\pi \otimes (\hat{y} \circ P_1))\left[(\theta, z) \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right] \right. \\&\qquad \left. + (1 - \lambda) (\pi \otimes (\hat{y} \circ P_2))\left[(\theta, z) \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right] \right) \\ &\ge \lambda \inf_{\hat{y} : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z} (\pi \otimes (\hat{y} \circ P_1))\left[(\theta, z) \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right] \\&\qquad + (1 - \lambda) \inf_{\hat{y} : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z} (\pi \otimes (\hat{y} \circ P_2))\left[(\theta, z) \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right] \\ &= \lambda \mathcal R_\pi^{P_1} + (1 - \lambda)\mathcal R_\pi^{P_2} \: . \end{align*} TODO: can we build kernels such that this lemma is a consequence of one of the lemmas above?

The Bayesian risk of a Markov kernel $\hat{y} : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z$ with respect to a prior $\pi \in \mathcal M(\Theta)$ on $(P, y, \ell')$ satisfies \begin{align*} R^P_\pi(\hat{y}) = ((P_\pi^\dagger \times \hat{y}) \circ P \circ \pi)\left[(\theta, z) \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right] \: , \end{align*} whenever the Bayesian inverse $P_\pi^\dagger$ of $P$ with respect to $\pi$ exists (Definition~\ref{def:bayesInv}).
nodes.label: lem:bayesianRisk_bayesInv

nodes.statement: Use the main property of the Bayesian inverse. \begin{align*} (P_\pi^\dagger \times \hat{y}) \circ P \circ \pi &= (\mathrm{id} \parallel \hat{y}) \circ (P_\pi^\dagger \times \mathrm{id}) \circ (P \circ \pi) \\ &= (\mathrm{id} \parallel \hat{y}) \circ (\mathrm{id} \times P) \circ \pi \\ &= (\mathrm{id} \times (\hat{y} \circ P)) \circ \pi \\ &= \pi \otimes (\hat{y} \circ P) \: . \end{align*}

The Bayesian risk of a Markov kernel $\hat{y} : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z$ with respect to a prior $\pi \in \mathcal M(\Theta)$ on $(P, y, \ell')$ satisfies \begin{align*} R^P_\pi(\hat{y}) \ge (P \circ \pi)\left[x \mapsto \inf_{z \in \mathcal Z} P_\pi^\dagger(x) \left[\theta \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right]\right] \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:bayesianRisk_ge_inf_bayesInv

nodes.statement: Starting from the equality of Lemma~\ref{lem:bayesianRisk_bayesInv}, we get \begin{align*} R^P_\pi(\hat{y}) &= ((P_\pi^\dagger \times \hat{y}) \circ P \circ \pi)\left[(\theta, z) \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right] \\ &= (P \circ \pi)\left[x \mapsto (P_\pi^\dagger(x) \times \hat{y}(x)) \left[(\theta, z) \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right]\right] \\ &= (P \circ \pi)\left[x \mapsto \hat{y}(x)\left[z \mapsto P_\pi^\dagger(x) \left[\theta \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right]\right]\right] \\ &\ge (P \circ \pi)\left[x \mapsto \inf_{z \in \mathcal Z} P_\pi^\dagger(x) \left[\theta \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right]\right] \: . \end{align*}

nodes.name: Generalized Bayes estimator
nodes.statement: The generalized Bayes estimator for prior $\pi \in \mathcal P(\Theta)$ on $(P, y, \ell')$ is the deterministic estimator $\mathcal X \to \mathcal Z$ given by \begin{align*} x \mapsto \arg\min_z P_\pi^\dagger(x)\left[\theta \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right] \: , \end{align*} if there exists such a measurable argmin.
nodes.label: def:genBayesEstimator

nodes.statement: The Bayesian risk of the generalized Bayes estimator $\hat{y}_B$ is \begin{align*} R^P_\pi(\hat{y}_B) = (P \circ \pi)\left[x \mapsto \inf_{z \in \mathcal Z} P_\pi^\dagger(x) \left[\theta \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right]\right] \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:bayesianRisk_genBayesEstimator

nodes.statement: Start from the equality of Lemma~\ref{lem:bayesianRisk_bayesInv} and use the definition of the generalized Bayes estimator.

When the generalized Bayes estimator is well defined, it is a Bayes estimator. The value of the Bayes risk with respect to the prior $\pi \in \mathcal M(\Theta)$ is then \begin{align*} \mathcal R^P_\pi = (P \circ \pi)\left[x \mapsto \inf_{z \in \mathcal Z} P_\pi^\dagger(x) \left[\theta \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right]\right] \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: thm:isBayesEstimator_genBayesEstimator

nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:bayesianRisk_ge_inf_bayesInv}, the Bayesian risk of the generalized Bayes estimator obtained in Lemma~\ref{lem:bayesianRisk_genBayesEstimator} is a lower bound for the Bayesian risk.

When the generalized Bayes estimator is well defined, the Bayes risk with respect to the prior $\pi \in \mathcal M(\Theta)$ is \begin{align*} \mathcal R^P_\pi = (P \circ \pi)\left[x \mapsto \inf_{z \in \mathcal Z} \pi \left[\theta \mapsto \frac{d P_\theta}{d (P \circ \pi)}(x) \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right]\right] \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:bayesRisk_eq_rnDeriv

nodes.statement: When the generalized Bayes estimator is well defined, the Bayes risk with respect to the prior $\pi \in \mathcal M(\Theta)$ for $\mathcal Y = \mathcal Z = \Theta$, $y = \mathrm{id}$ and $\ell' = \mathbb{I}\{\theta \ne z\}$ is \begin{align*} \mathcal R^P_\pi = (P \circ \pi)[1] - (P \circ \pi)\left[x \mapsto \sup_{z \in \mathcal Z} P_\pi^\dagger(x) \{z\}\right] \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:bayesRisk_binary_eq_sub_bayesInv

nodes.statement: When the generalized Bayes estimator is well defined, the Bayes risk with respect to the prior $\pi \in \mathcal M(\Theta)$ for $\mathcal Y = \mathcal Z = \Theta$, $y = \mathrm{id}$ and $\ell' = \mathbb{I}\{\theta \ne z\}$ is \begin{align*} \mathcal R^P_\pi = (P \circ \pi)[1] - (P \circ \pi)\left[x \mapsto \sup_{z \in \mathcal Z} \frac{d P_z}{d (P \circ \pi)}(x) \pi\{z\} \right] \: . \end{align*} When $\pi$ is a probability measure and $P$ is a Markov kernel, $(P \circ \pi)[1] = 1$.
nodes.label: lem:bayesRisk_binary_eq_sub

nodes.statement: The generalized Bayes estimator for prior $\pi \in \mathcal P(\Theta)$ on the estimation problem defined by $\mathcal Y = \mathcal Z = \Theta$, $y = \mathrm{id}$ and $\ell' = \mathbb{I}\{\theta \ne z\}$ is \begin{align*} x \mapsto \arg\max_z \left( \pi\{z\} \frac{d P_z}{d (P \circ \pi)}(x) \right) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:genBayesEstimator_binary

nodes.statement: Suppose that $\Theta$ is finite and let $\xi \in \mathcal P(\Theta)$. The Bayes risk with respect to the prior $\pi \in \mathcal P(\Theta)$ for $\mathcal Y = \mathcal Z = \Theta$, $y = \mathrm{id}$, $P$ a Markov kernel and $\ell' = \mathbb{I}\{\theta \ne z\}$ satisfies \begin{align*} \mathcal R^P_\pi \le 1 - \left(\prod_{\theta \in \Theta} \pi_\theta^{\xi_\theta}\right) (P \circ \pi)\left[x \mapsto \prod_{\theta \in \Theta} \left(\frac{d P_\theta}{d (P \circ \pi)}(x)\right)^{\xi_\theta} \right] \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:bayesRisk_binary_le_sub_prod

nodes.statement: The Bayes risk increase $I^P_{\pi}(\kappa)$ of a kernel $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X'$ with respect to the estimation problem $(P, y, \ell')$ and the prior $\pi \in \mathcal M(\Theta)$ is the difference of the Bayes risk of $(\kappa \circ P, y, \ell')$ and that of $(P, y, \ell')$. That is, \begin{align*} I^P_{\pi}(\kappa) &= \mathcal R^{\kappa \circ P}_\pi - \mathcal R^P_\pi \\ &= \inf_{\hat{y} : \mathcal X' \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z} (\pi \otimes (\hat{y} \circ \kappa \circ P))\left[(\theta, z) \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right] - \inf_{\hat{y} : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z} (\pi \otimes (\hat{y} \circ P))\left[(\theta, z) \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right] \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: def:riskIncrease

nodes.statement: For $\kappa$ a Markov kernel, $I^P_\pi(\kappa) \ge 0$~.
nodes.label: lem:riskIncrease_nonneg

nodes.statement: Use Theorem~\ref{thm:data_proc_bayesRisk}.

For $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X'$ and $\eta : \mathcal X' \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X''$ two Markov kernels, $I^P_\pi(\eta \circ \kappa) = I^P_\pi(\kappa) + I^{\kappa \circ P}_\pi(\eta)$~.
nodes.label: lem:riskIncrease_comp

nodes.statement: \begin{align*} I^P_\pi(\kappa) + I^{\kappa \circ P}_\pi(\eta) &= \mathcal R^{\kappa \circ P}_\pi - \mathcal R^{P}_\pi + \mathcal R^{\eta \circ \kappa \circ P}_\pi - \mathcal R^{\kappa \circ P}_\pi \\ &= \mathcal R^{\eta \circ \kappa \circ P}_\pi - \mathcal R^{P}_\pi \\ &= I^P_\pi(\eta \circ \kappa) \: . \end{align*}

nodes.name: Data-processing inequality
nodes.statement: For any measurable space $\mathcal X$, let $d_{\mathcal X} : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow *$ be the Markov kernel to the point space. For all Markov kernels $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X'$, \begin{align*} I_\pi^P(d_{\mathcal X}) \ge I_\pi^{\kappa \circ P}(d_{\mathcal X'}) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:riskIncrease_comp_del

nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:riskIncrease_comp}, then Lemma~\ref{lem:riskIncrease_nonneg}, \begin{align*} I_\pi^P(d_{\mathcal X'} \circ \kappa) = I^P_\pi(\kappa) + I^{\kappa \circ P}_\pi(d_{\mathcal X'}) \ge I_\pi^{\kappa \circ P}(d_{\mathcal X'}) \: . \end{align*} Finally, $d_{\mathcal X'} \circ \kappa = d_{\mathcal X}$ since $\kappa$ is a Markov kernel.

The Bayesian inverse of a kernel $P : \{0,1\} \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$ with respect to a prior $\xi \in \mathcal M(\{0,1\})$ is $P_\xi^\dagger(x) = \left(\xi_0\frac{d P(0)}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x), \xi_1\frac{d P(1)}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x)\right)$ (almost surely w.r.t. $P \circ \xi = \xi_0 P(0) + \xi_1 P(1)$).
nodes.label: lem:bayesInv_binary

nodes.statement: For $\Theta = \{0,1\}$, the Bayes risk of a prior $\xi \in \mathcal M(\{0,1\})$ is \begin{align*} \mathcal R^P_\xi = (P \circ \xi)\left[x \mapsto \inf_{z \in \mathcal Z} \left( \xi_0\frac{d P(0)}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x)\ell'(y(0), z) + \xi_1\frac{d P(1)}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x)\ell'(y(1), z) \right) \right] \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:bayesRisk_binary

nodes.statement: Use Theorem~\ref{thm:isBayesEstimator_genBayesEstimator}, with the value of $P_\xi^\dagger$ given by Lemma~\ref{lem:bayesInv_binary}.

nodes.statement: For all $a, b > 0$, $\mathcal B_\xi(\mu, \nu) = \mathcal B_{(a \xi_0, b \xi_1)}(a^{-1} \mu, b^{-1} \nu)$~.

nodes.label: lem:bayesBinaryRisk_one_one

Let $d_{\mathcal X} : \mathcal X ightsquigarrow *$ be the discard kernel and $\delta_*$ be the only probability measure over $*$, that is a Dirac delta. Then applying the DPI (Theorem~ef{thm:data_proc_bayesBinaryRisk}), followed by Lemma~ef{lem:bayesBinaryRisk_mul} and Lemma~ef{lem:bayesBinaryRisk_self}, we obtain:  egin{align*} \mathcal B_\xi(\mu,

nodes.label: lem:bayesBinaryRisk_symm

nodes.statement: The generalized Bayes estimator for the Bayes binary risk with prior $\xi \in \mathcal M(\{0,1\})$ is $x \mapsto \text{if } \xi_1\frac{d \nu}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x) \le \xi_0\frac{d \mu}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x) \text{ then } 0 \text{ else } 1$, i.e. it is equal to $\mathbb{I}_E$ for $E = \{x \mid \xi_1\frac{d \nu}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x) > \xi_0\frac{d \mu}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x)\}$~.
nodes.label: lem:genBayesEstimator_bayesBinaryRisk

nodes.statement: The generalized Bayes estimator is defined by \begin{align*} x \mapsto \arg\min_z P_\xi^\dagger(x)\left[\theta \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right] \: . \end{align*} For the simple binary hypothesis testing problem, \begin{align*} P_\xi^\dagger(x)\left[\theta \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right] &= P_\xi^\dagger(x)(\theta \ne z) \: . \end{align*} For $z = 0$, this is $P_\xi^\dagger(x)(\{1\})$ and for $z = 1$, this is $P_\xi^\dagger(x)(\{0\})$. The generalized Bayes estimator is $x \mapsto \text{if } P_\xi^\dagger(x)(\{1\}) \le P_\xi^\dagger(x)(\{0\}) \text{ then } 0 \text{ else } 1$. The expression of the lemma statement is obtained by replacing $P_\xi^\dagger$ by its value (Lemma~\ref{lem:bayesInv_binary}).
\begin{align*} \mathcal B_\xi(\mu, \nu) = \inf_{E \text{ event}} \left( \xi_0 \mu(E) + \xi_1 \nu(E^c) \right) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:bayesBinaryRisk_eq_event

nodes.statement:
By definition,  egin{align*} \mathcal B_\xi(\mu, 
u) = \inf_{\hat{y} : \mathcal X ightsquigarrow \{0,1\}}\left(\xi_0 (\hat{y} \circ \mu)(\{1\}) + \xi_1 (\hat{y} \circ 
u)(\{0\})ight) \: . \end{align*} If we restrict the infimum to deterministic kernels corresponding to functions of the form $x \mapsto \mathbb{I}\{x \in E\}$, we get that $\mathcal B_\xi(\mu, 
u)$ is bounded from above by the expression for which we want to show equality. Since the Bayes estimator has that shape (Lemma~ef{lem:genBayesEstimator_bayesBinaryRisk}), $\mathcal B_\xi(\mu, 
u)$ is also greater than the infimum and we have equality.

The Bayes risk of simple binary hypothesis testing for prior $\xi \in \mathcal M(\{0,1\})$ is \begin{align*} \mathcal B_\xi(\mu, \nu) = (P \circ \xi)\left[x \mapsto \min \left\{\xi_0\frac{d \mu}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x), \xi_1\frac{d \nu}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x)\right\}\right] \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: thm:bayesBinaryRisk_eq

nodes.statement: By Theorem~\ref{thm:isBayesEstimator_genBayesEstimator}, the generalized Bayes estimator is a Bayes estimator, hence it suffices to compute its Bayesian risk. By Lemma~\ref{lem:bayesianRisk_genBayesEstimator}, \begin{align*} R_\xi(\hat{y}_B) &= (P \circ \xi)\left[x \mapsto \inf_{z \in \mathcal Z} P_\xi^\dagger(x) \left[\theta \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right]\right] \\ &= (P \circ \xi)\left[x \mapsto \min \left\{P_\xi^\dagger(x)(\{0\}), P_\xi^\dagger(x)(\{1\})\right\}\right] \\ &= (P \circ \xi)\left[x \mapsto \min \left\{\xi_0\frac{d \mu}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x), \xi_1\frac{d \nu}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x)\right\}\right] \: . \end{align*} The last line is obtained by replacing $P_\xi^\dagger$ by its value (Lemma~\ref{lem:bayesInv_binary}).

\begin{align*} \mathcal B_\xi(\mu, \nu) = \frac{1}{2}\left((P \circ \xi)(\mathcal X) - (P \circ \xi)\left[x \mapsto \left\vert \xi_0\frac{d \mu}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x) - \xi_1\frac{d \nu}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x)\right\vert\right] \right) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: cor:bayesBinaryRisk_eq_abs

nodes.statement: Use Theorem~\ref{thm:bayesBinaryRisk_eq} and the equality $\min\{a,b\} = \frac{1}{2}(a + b - \vert a - b \vert)$.

Let $\hat{y}_B$ be the generalized Bayes estimator for simple binary hypothesis testing. The distribution $\ell \circ (\mathrm{id} \parallel \hat{y}_B) \circ (\pi \otimes P)$ (in which $\ell$ stands for the associated deterministic kernel) is a Bernoulli with mean $\mathcal B_\pi(\mu, \nu)$.
nodes.label: lem:bayesBinaryRisk_bernoulli

nodes.statement: $\ell$ takes values in $\{0,1\}$ so the law has to be Bernoulli. It has mean $\mathcal B_\pi(\mu, \nu)$ because the expected risk of the generalized Bayes estimator is $\mathcal B_\pi(\mu, \nu)$.

nodes.name: Divergence
nodes.statement: A divergence between measures is a function $D$ which for any measurable space $\mathcal X$ and any two measures $\mu, \nu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$, returns a value $D(\mu, \nu) \in \mathbb{R} \cup \{+\infty\}$.
nodes.label: def:div

nodes.name: Data-processing inequality
nodes.statement:
A divergence $D$ is said to satisfy the data-processing inequality (DPI) if for all measurable spaces $\mathcal X, \mathcal Y$, all $\mu, 
u \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ and all Markov kernels $\kappa : \mathcal X ightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$,  egin{align*} D(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ 
u) \le D(\mu, 
u) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: def:dpi

nodes.name: Second marginal
nodes.statement:
Let $D$ be a divergence that satisfies the DPI. Let $\mathcal \mu, 
u \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ and let $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X ightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$. Then  egin{align*} D(\kappa \circ \mu, \eta \circ 
u) \le D(\mu \otimes \kappa, 
u \otimes \eta) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:div_comp_le_div_compProd

nodes.statement: Use the DPI for the deterministic kernel of the function $(x,y) \mapsto y$.

nodes.name: First marginal
nodes.statement:
Let $D$ be a divergence that satisfies the DPI. Let $\mathcal \mu, 
u \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ and let $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X ightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be Markov kernels. Then  egin{align*} D(\mu, 
u) \le D(\mu \otimes \kappa, 
u \otimes \eta) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:div_le_div_compProd

nodes.statement: Use the DPI for the deterministic kernel of the function $(x,y) \mapsto x$.

Let $D$ be a divergence that satisfies the DPI. Let $\mathcal \mu, 
u \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ and let $\kappa : \mathcal X ightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be a Markov kernel. Then  egin{align*} D(\mu \otimes \kappa, 
u \otimes \kappa) = D(\mu, 
u) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:div_compProd_right

nodes.statement: Lemma~\ref{lem:div_le_div_compProd} gives one inequality. The other inequality is the DPI: $\mu \otimes \kappa = (\mathrm{id} \times \kappa) \circ \mu$.

nodes.name: Conditional divergence
nodes.statement: Let $D$ be a divergence. The conditional divergence of kernels $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ with respect to a measure $\mu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ is $\mu[x \mapsto D(\kappa(x), \eta(x)]$. It is denoted by $D(\kappa, \eta \mid \mu)$.
nodes.label: def:condDiv

nodes.name: Conditioning increases divergence
nodes.statement: Let $D$ be a divergence that satisfies the DPI and for which $D(\kappa, \eta \mid \mu) = D(\mu \otimes \kappa, \mu \otimes \eta)$. Let $\mathcal \mu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ and let $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be Markov kernels. Then \begin{align*} D(\kappa \circ \mu, \eta \circ \mu) \le D(\kappa, \eta \mid \mu) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:div_comp_le_div_compProd_right

nodes.statement: This is a special case of Lemma~\ref{lem:div_comp_le_div_compProd}.

nodes.name: Data-processing inequality
nodes.statement:
For $\mu, 
u \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$, $\xi \in \mathcal M(\{0,1\})$ and $\kappa : \mathcal X ightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ a Markov kernel, $\mathcal I_\xi(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ 
u) \le \mathcal I_\xi(\mu, 
u)$~.
nodes.label: thm:data_proc_statInfo

nodes.statement:
Since $\kappa$ is a Markov kernel,  egin{align*} \mathcal I_\xi(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ 
u) &= \min\{\xi_0(\kappa \circ \mu)(\mathcal X), \xi_1(\kappa \circ 
u)(\mathcal X)\} - \mathcal B_\xi(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ 
u) \ &= \min\{\xi_0 \mu(\mathcal X), \xi_1 
u(\mathcal X)\} - \mathcal B_\xi(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ 
u) \end{align*} It suffices to prove $\mathcal B_\xi(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ 
u) \ge \mathcal B_\xi(\mu, 
u)$ since $\mathcal I_\xi(\mu, 
u) = \min\{\xi_0\mu(\mathcal X), \xi_1
u(\mathcal X)\} - \mathcal B_\xi(\mu, 
u)$. The inequality was proved in Theorem~ef{thm:data_proc_bayesBinaryRisk}. Alternatively, we can use Lemma~ef{lem:riskIncrease_comp_del}.

Let $\mu, 
u$ be two measures on $\mathcal X$, $\xi \in \mathcal M(\{0,1\})$ and let $E$ be an event on $\mathcal X$. Let $\mu_E$ and $
u_E$ be the two Bernoulli distributions with respective means $\mu(E)$ and $
u(E)$. Then $\mathcal I_\xi(\mu, 
u) \ge \mathcal I_\xi(\mu_E, 
u_E)$.
nodes.label: cor:statInfo_data_proc_event

nodes.statement: Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:data_proc_statInfo} to the deterministic kernel $\mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \{0,1\}$ given by the function $x \mapsto \mathbb{I}\{x \in E\}$.

For finite measures $\mu, 
u$ and $\xi \in \mathcal M(\{0,1\})$, for any measure $\zeta$ with $\mu \ll \zeta$ and $
u \ll \zeta$~,  egin{align*} \mathcal I_\xi(\mu, 
u) &= \min\{\xi_0\mu(\mathcal X), \xi_1
u(\mathcal X)\} - \zeta\left[x \mapsto \min \left\{\xi_0 rac{d \mu}{d\zeta}(x), \xi_1 rac{d 
u}{d\zeta}(x)ight\}ight] \: . \end{align*} This holds in particular for $\zeta = P \circ \xi$.
nodes.label: lem:statInfo_eq_sub_min

nodes.statement: Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:bayesBinaryRisk_eq} to get that result for $\zeta = P \circ \xi$. Then for other $\zeta$ with $\mu \ll \zeta$ and $\nu \ll \zeta$~, use $\frac{d \mu}{d\zeta} = \frac{d \mu}{d(P \circ \xi)} / \frac{d (P \circ \xi)}{d\zeta}$~.

For finite measures $\mu, 
u$ and $\xi \in \mathcal M(\{0,1\})$, for any measure $\zeta$ with $\mu \ll \zeta$ and $
u \ll \zeta$~,  egin{align*} \mathcal I_\xi(\mu, 
u) &= -  rac{1}{2} \left\vert \xi_0\mu(\mathcal X) - \xi_1
u(\mathcal X) ight\vert +  rac{1}{2} \zeta\left[x \mapsto \left\vert \xi_0 rac{d \mu}{d\zeta}(x) - \xi_1 rac{d 
u}{d\zeta}(x)ight\vertight] \: . \end{align*} This holds in particular for $\zeta = P \circ \xi$.
nodes.label: lem:statInfo_eq_integral_abs_sub

nodes.statement: Apply Corollary~\ref{cor:bayesBinaryRisk_eq_abs} and write $\min\{\xi_0\mu(\mathcal X), \xi_1\nu(\mathcal X)\} = \frac{1}{2}\left((P \circ \xi)(\mathcal X) - \left\vert \xi_0\mu(\mathcal X) - \xi_1\nu(\mathcal X) \right\vert \right)$ to get the result for $\zeta = P \circ \xi$. The result for other $\zeta$ follows from simple manipulations of Radon-Nikodym derivatives.

nodes.name: Integral form of the statistical information
nodes.statement:
For finite measures $\mu, 
u$ and $\xi \in \mathcal M(\{0,1\})$,  egin{align*} \mathcal I_\xi(\mu, 
u) &= 
u\left[ x \mapsto \max \left\{0 , \xi_0 rac{d \mu}{d
u}(x) - \xi_1 ight\} ight] + \xi_0 \mu_{\perp 
u}(\mathcal X) & 	ext{ if } \xi_0 \mu(\mathcal X) \le \xi_1 
u(\mathcal X) \: , \ \mathcal I_\xi(\mu, 
u) &= 
u\left[ x \mapsto \max \left\{0 , \xi_1 - \xi_0 rac{d \mu}{d
u}(x) ight\} ight] & 	ext{ if } \xi_0 \mu(\mathcal X) \ge \xi_1 
u(\mathcal X) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: thm:statInfo_eq_integral

nodes.statement:
By Theorem~ef{thm:bayesBinaryRisk_eq},  egin{align*} \mathcal I_\xi(\mu, 
u) &= \min\{\xi_0\mu(\mathcal X), \xi_1
u(\mathcal X)\} - (P \circ \xi)\left[x \mapsto \min \left\{\xi_0 rac{d \mu}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x), \xi_1 rac{d 
u}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x)ight\}ight] \: . \end{align*} Suppose that $\xi_0\mu(\mathcal X) \le \xi_1
u(\mathcal X)$~. Then  egin{align*} \mathcal I_\xi(\mu, 
u) &= \xi_0\mu(\mathcal X) - (P \circ \xi)\left[x \mapsto \xi_0 rac{d \mu}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x) + \min \left\{0 , \xi_1 rac{d 
u}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x) - \xi_0 rac{d \mu}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x)ight\}ight] \ &= - (P \circ \xi)\left[x \mapsto \min \left\{0 , \xi_1 rac{d 
u}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x) - \xi_0 rac{d \mu}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x) ight\}ight] \ &= (P \circ \xi)\left[x \mapsto \max \left\{0 , \xi_0 rac{d \mu}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x) - \xi_1 rac{d 
u}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x) ight\}ight] \ &= 
u\left[ x \mapsto \max \left\{0 , \xi_0 rac{d \mu}{d
u}(x) - \xi_1 ight\} ight] + \xi_0 \mu_{\perp 
u}(\mathcal X) \: . \end{align*} If on the other hand $\xi_0\mu(\mathcal X) \ge \xi_1
u(\mathcal X)$~, with similar computations,  egin{align*} \mathcal I_\xi(\mu, 
u) &= (P \circ \xi)\left[x \mapsto \max \left\{0 , \xi_1 rac{d 
u}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x) - \xi_0 rac{d \mu}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x) ight\}ight] \ &= 
u\left[ x \mapsto \max \left\{0 , \xi_1 - \xi_0 rac{d \mu}{d
u}(x) ight\} ight] \: . \end{align*}

For finite measures $\mu, 
u$ and $\xi \in \mathcal M(\{0,1\})$,  egin{align*} \mathcal I_\xi(\mu, 
u) &= - rac{1}{2} \left\vert\xi_0 \mu(\mathcal X) - \xi_1 
u(\mathcal X)ight\vert +  rac{1}{2}\left( 
u\left[ x \mapsto \left\vert\xi_0 rac{d \mu}{d
u}(x) - \xi_1 ight\vert ight] + \xi_0 \mu_{\perp 
u}(\mathcal X)ight) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: cor:statInfo_eq_integral_abs

nodes.statement: Start from Theorem~\ref{thm:statInfo_eq_integral}, then use $\max\{a,b\} = \frac{1}{2}\left( a + b + \vert a - b \vert \right)$~. The two cases of Theorem~\ref{thm:statInfo_eq_integral} lead to the same expression.

For finite measures $\mu, 
u$ and $\xi \in \mathcal M(\{0,1\})$,  egin{align*} \mathcal I_\xi(\mu, 
u) &= \min\{\xi_0 \mu(\mathcal X), \xi_1 
u(\mathcal X)\} - \inf_{E 	ext{ event}} \left( \xi_0 \mu(E) + \xi_1 
u(E^c) ight) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:statInfo_eq_sub_inf_event

nodes.statement: This is a direct application of Lemma~\ref{lem:bayesBinaryRisk_eq_event}.

For finite measures $\mu, 
u$ and $\xi \in \mathcal M(\{0,1\})$,  egin{align*} \mathcal I_\xi(\mu, 
u) &= - \max\{0, \xi_1 
u(\mathcal X) - \xi_0 \mu(\mathcal X) \} + \sup_{E 	ext{ event}} \left( \xi_1 
u(E) - \xi_0 \mu(E) ight) \ &= - \max\{0, \xi_0 \mu(\mathcal X) - \xi_1 
u(\mathcal X) \} + \sup_{E 	ext{ event}} \left( \xi_0 \mu(E) - \xi_1 
u(E) ight) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:statInfo_eq_sup_event

nodes.statement:
The DeGroot statistical information between finite measures $\mu$ and $
u$ for $\pi \in [0,1]$ is $I_\pi (\mu, 
u) = \mathcal I_{(\pi, 1 - \pi)}(\mu, 
u)$~.
nodes.label: def:deGrootInfo

nodes.statement:
The $E_\gamma$ or hockey-stick divergence between finite measures $\mu$ and $
u$ for $\gamma \in (0,+\infty)$ is $E_\gamma(\mu, 
u) = \mathcal I_{(1,\gamma)}(\mu, 
u)$~.
nodes.label: def:eGamma

nodes.statement:
The total variation distance between finite measures $\mu$ and $
u$ is $\mathrm{TV}(\mu, 
u) = \mathcal I_{(1,1)}(\mu, 
u)$~.
nodes.label: def:TV

nodes.label: lem:tv_self

For $\mu, 
u \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$, $\mathrm{TV}(\mu, 
u) \le \min\{\mu(\mathcal X), 
u(\mathcal X)\}$~.

nodes.statement: Use Lemma~\ref{lem:statInfo_le}.

nodes.statement:

u \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ and $\kappa : \mathcal X ightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ a Markov kernel, $\mathrm{TV}(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ 
u) \le \mathrm{TV}(\mu, 
u)$~.

For finite measures $\mu, 
u$, for any measure $\zeta$ with $\mu \ll \zeta$ and $
u \ll \zeta$~,  egin{align*} \mathrm{TV}(\mu, 
u) &= \min\{\mu(\mathcal X), 
u(\mathcal X)\} - \zeta\left[x \mapsto \min \left\{ rac{d \mu}{d\zeta}(x),  rac{d 
u}{d\zeta}(x)ight\}ight] \: . \end{align*} This holds in particular for $\zeta = P \circ \xi$.
nodes.label: lem:tv_eq_sub_min

nodes.statement: Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:statInfo_eq_sub_min}.

For finite measures $\mu, 
u$, for any measure $\zeta$ with $\mu \ll \zeta$ and $
u \ll \zeta$~,  egin{align*} \mathrm{TV}(\mu, 
u) &= -  rac{1}{2} \left\vert \mu(\mathcal X) - 
u(\mathcal X) ight\vert +  rac{1}{2} \zeta\left[x \mapsto \left\vert  rac{d \mu}{d\zeta}(x) -  rac{d 
u}{d\zeta}(x)ight\vertight] \: . \end{align*} This holds in particular for $\zeta = P \circ \xi$.
nodes.label: lem:tv_eq_integral_abs_sub

nodes.statement: Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:statInfo_eq_integral_abs_sub}.

nodes.statement:
For finite measures $\mu, 
u$,  egin{align*} \mathrm{TV}(\mu, 
u) &= 
u\left[ x \mapsto \max \left\{0 ,  rac{d \mu}{d
u}(x) - 1 ight\} ight] + \mu_{\perp 
u}(\mathcal X) & 	ext{ if } \mu(\mathcal X) \le 
u(\mathcal X) \: , \ \mathrm{TV}(\mu, 
u) &= 
u\left[ x \mapsto \max \left\{0 , 1 -  rac{d \mu}{d
u}(x) ight\} ight] & 	ext{ if } \mu(\mathcal X) \ge 
u(\mathcal X) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:tv_eq_integral

nodes.statement: Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:statInfo_eq_integral}.

For finite measures $\mu, 
u$,  egin{align*} \mathrm{TV}(\mu, 
u) &= - rac{1}{2} \left\vert \mu(\mathcal X) - 
u(\mathcal X)ight\vert +  rac{1}{2}\left( 
u\left[ x \mapsto \left\vert  rac{d \mu}{d
u}(x) - 1 ight\vert ight] + \mu_{\perp 
u}(\mathcal X)ight) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:tv_eq_integral_abs

nodes.statement: Apply Corollary~\ref{cor:statInfo_eq_integral_abs}.

For finite measures $\mu, 
u$,  egin{align*} \mathrm{TV}(\mu, 
u) &= \min\{\mu(\mathcal X), 
u(\mathcal X)\} - \inf_{E 	ext{ event}} \left( \mu(E) + 
u(E^c) ight) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:tv_eq_sub_inf_event

nodes.statement: Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:statInfo_eq_sub_inf_event}.

Let $\mu, 
u$ be two finite measures on $\mathcal X$ with $\mu(\mathcal X) \leq 
u(\mathcal X)$.\ Then $TV(\mu, 
u) = \sup_{E 	ext{ event}} \left( \mu(E) - 
u(E) ight)$.
nodes.label: thm:tv_eq_sup_sub_measure

nodes.statement:
Starting from Lemma~ef{lem:tv_eq_sub_inf_event},  egin{align*} \mathrm{TV}(\mu, 
u) &= \min\{\mu(\mathcal X), 
u(\mathcal X)\} - \inf_{E 	ext{ event}} \left( \mu(E) + 
u(E^c) ight) \ &= \mu(\mathcal X) - \inf_{E 	ext{ event}} \left( \mu(E^c) + 
u(E) ight) \ &= \mu(\mathcal X) - \mu(\mathcal X) - \inf_{E 	ext{ event}} \left( -\mu(E) + 
u(E) ight) \ &= \sup_{E 	ext{ event}} \left( \mu(E) - 
u(E) ight) \: . \end{align*}

Let $\mathcal F = \{f : \mathcal X 	o \mathbb{R} \mid \Vert f \Vert_\infty \le 1\}$. Then for $\mu, 
u$ finite measures with $\mu(\mathcal X) = 
u(\mathcal X)$, $ rac{1}{2} \sup_{f \in \mathcal F} \left( \mu[f] - 
u[f] ight) \le \mathrm{TV}(\mu, 
u)$.
nodes.label: lem:tv_eq_sup_aux

nodes.statement:
Let $p,q$ be the respective densities of $\mu, 
u$ with respect to $\xi=\mu+
u$. For any $f \in \mathcal F$,  egin{align*} \mu[f] - 
u[f] = \int_x f(x)(p(x) - q(x)) \partial\xi &\le \int_x \Vert f(x) \Vert_\infty \vert p(x) - q(x) \vert \partial\xi \ &\le \int_x \vert p(x) - q(x) \vert \partial\xi = 2 \mathrm{TV}(\mu, 
u) \: . \end{align*} The last equality is Lemma~ef{lem:tv_eq_integral_abs_sub}.

Let $\mathcal F = \{f : \mathcal X 	o \mathbb{R} \mid \Vert f \Vert_\infty \le 1\}$. Then for $\mu, 
u$ finite measures with $\mu(\mathcal X) = 
u(\mathcal X)$, $\mathrm{TV}(\mu, 
u) =  rac{1}{2} \sup_{f \in \mathcal F} \left( \mu[f] - 
u[f] ight)$.
nodes.label: thm:tv_eq_sup_sub_integral

nodes.statement: Lemma~\ref{lem:tv_eq_sup_aux} gives $\mathrm{TV}(\mu, \nu) \ge \frac{1}{2} \sup_{f \in \mathcal F} \left( \mu[f] - \nu[f] \right)$. The bayes estimator is a function of the form $x \mapsto \mathbb{I}\{x \in E\}$ for some event $E$, hence it belongs to $\mathcal F$. This gives equality.

Let $\mu, 
u$ be two measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $E$ be an event. Let $\mu_E$ and $
u_E$ be the two Bernoulli distributions with respective means $\mu(E)$ and $
u(E)$. Then $\mathrm{TV}(\mu, 
u) \ge \mathrm{TV}(\mu_E, 
u_E)$.
nodes.label: lem:tv_data_proc_event

u\left[x \mapsto f\left( rac{d \mu}{d

nodes.name: Curvature measure
nodes.statement: Let $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a convex function. Then its right derivative $f'_+(x) \coloneqq \lim_{y \downarrow x}\frac{f(y) - f(x)}{y - x}$ is a Stieltjes function (a monotone right continuous function) and it defines a measure $\gamma_f$ on $\mathbb{R}$ by $\gamma_f((x,y]) \coloneqq f'_+(y) - f'_+(x)$~. \cite{liese2012phi} calls $\gamma_f$ the curvature measure of $f$.
nodes.label: def:curvatureMeasure

nodes.statement: For $a > 0$ and $f$ a convex function, the curvature measure of $af$ is $\gamma_{af} = a \gamma_f$~.
nodes.label: lem:curvatureMeasure_mul

nodes.statement: The right derivative of $af$ is $a f'_+$ (with values in $[-\infty, +\infty]$), hence $\gamma_{af}((x,y]) = a f'_+(y) - a f'_+(x) = a \gamma_f((x,y])$. The equality of the measures is obtained at the level of the outer measures, which are built from these interval lengths. For $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, the case $a = 0$ is trivial. It fails in the Lean formalization, where the right derivative is $-\infty$ to the left of the domain of $f$: $0 \cdot f$ is the zero function on $[0, +\infty)$, whose right derivative jumps from $-\infty$ to $0$ at $0$, so that $\gamma_{0 \cdot f}$ has an infinite atom at $0$.

Let $f,g$ be two convex functions whose effective domains have the same endpoints $a \le b$, and such that the right derivatives $f'_+$ and $g'_+$ either both tend to $-\infty$ at $a$ or both have a finite limit at $a$. Then the curvature measure of $f+g$ is $\gamma_{f+g} = \gamma_f + \gamma_g$~. In particular, this holds for $f,g: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ two convex functions.
nodes.label: lem:curvatureMeasure_add

nodes.statement: The right derivative of $f+g$ is $f'_+ + g'_+$, seen as functions with values in $[-\infty, +\infty]$ ($-\infty$ below the domain, $+\infty$ above it). By the assumptions, $f'_+$ and $g'_+$ are equal to $-\infty$ at the same points and equal to $+\infty$ at the same points. On the region where both are finite, $\gamma_{f+g}((x,y]) = \gamma_f((x,y]) + \gamma_g((x,y])$. The region where $f'_+$ and $g'_+$ are $-\infty$, and the region above the first point where they are $+\infty$, are null for the three measures. At $a$ and $b$, the three measures have the same atoms (equal to $0$ or $+\infty$). The assumption at $a$ is needed: if $f'_+(x) \to -\infty$ as $x \downarrow a$ but $g'_+$ has a finite limit at $a$, then $\gamma_g$ has an infinite atom at $a$ but $\gamma_{f+g}$ does not.

If $f$ and $g$ are two Stieltjes functions with associated measures $\mu_f$ and $\mu_g$ and $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$, then \begin{align*} \int_x f(x) \partial\mu_g = f(b)g(b) - f(a)g(a) - \int_x g(x) \partial\mu_f \: . \end{align*}

nodes.statement: Let $\Lambda$ be the Lebesgue measure and let $x < y$. Since $f$ has right derivative $f'_+$ in $(x,y)$ and $f'_+$ is integrable on that interval, \begin{align*} f(y) - f(x) = \int_{z \in (x, y]} f'_+(z) \partial \Lambda \: . \end{align*} We now integrate by parts, using Theorem~\ref{thm:integration_by_parts}. $\Lambda$ is the measure obtained from the Stieltjes function $z \mapsto z - y$. \begin{align*} \int_{z \in (x, y]} f'_+(z) \partial \Lambda &= - \int_{z \in (x,y]} (z - y)\partial \gamma_f + f'_+(y)(y - y) - f'_+(x)(x - y) \\ &= \int_{z \in (x,y]} (y - z)\partial \gamma_f + f'_+(x)(y - x) \: . \end{align*} Putting the two equalities together, we get the result for $x < y$. The proof for $x > y$ is similar, and for $x = y$ both sides of both equations are zero.

nodes.statement:
Note that from the hypothesis it easily follows that $\mu \ll 
u$ and $\mu$-a.e.\ $\kappa(x) \ll \eta(x)$. Applying Lemma~ef{lem:integrable_fDiv_compProd_iff} we know that $\log  rac{d \mu \otimes \kappa}{d 
u \otimes \eta}$ is $
u \otimes \eta$-integrable iff the following hold:  egin{enumerate} \item[i.] for $
u$-almost all $x$, $y \mapsto  rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x)  rac{d \kappa(x)}{d \eta(x)}(y) \log \left( rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x)  rac{d \kappa(x)}{d \eta(x)}(y) ight) $ is $\eta(x)$-integrable \item[ii.] $x \mapsto \int_y  rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x)  rac{d \kappa(x)}{d \eta(x)}(y) \log \left( rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x)  rac{d \kappa(x)}{d \eta(x)}(y) ight) \partial \eta (x)$ is $
u$-integrable \end{enumerate} { fseries(i.$\Leftarrow$)} 3.\ implies that $
u$-a.e.\ $y \mapsto  rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x) \log  rac{d \kappa(x)}{d \eta(x)}(y)$ is $\kappa(x)$-integrable, hence $y \mapsto  rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x)  rac{d \kappa(x)}{d \eta(x)}(y) \log  rac{d \kappa(x)}{d \eta(x)}(y)$ is $\eta(x)$-integrable $
u$-a.e.\ Moreover $y \mapsto  rac{d \kappa(x)}{d \eta(x)}(y)$ is $\eta(x)$-integrable, then, since $ rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x) \log  rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x)$ is constant in $y$, $y \mapsto  rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x)  rac{d \kappa(x)}{d \eta(x)}(y) \log  rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x)$ is $\eta(x)$-integrable. This allows us to conclude that $y \mapsto  rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x)  rac{d \kappa(x)}{d \eta(x)}(y) \log  rac{d \kappa(x)}{d \eta(x)}(y) +  rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x)  rac{d \kappa(x)}{d \eta(x)}(y) \log  rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x) =  rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x)  rac{d \kappa(x)}{d \eta(x)}(y) \log \left( rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x)  rac{d \kappa(x)}{d \eta(x)}(y) ight)$ is $\eta(x)$-integrable $
u$-a.e. { fseries(ii.$\Leftarrow$)} 1.\ implies that $x \mapsto  rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x) \log  rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x)$ is $
u$-integrable. 2.\ implies that $x \mapsto  rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x) \int_y  rac{d \kappa(x)}{d \eta(x)}(y) \log  rac{d \kappa(x)}{d \eta(x)}(y) \partial \eta(x)$ is $
u$-integrable. Therefore $$x \mapsto  rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x) \log  rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x) +  rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x) \int_y  rac{d \kappa(x)}{d \eta(x)}(y) \log  rac{d \kappa(x)}{d \eta(x)}(y) \partial \eta(x) = \int_y  rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x)  rac{d \kappa(x)}{d \eta(x)}(y) \log \left( rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x)  rac{d \kappa(x)}{d \eta(x)}(y) ight) \partial \eta (x)$$ is $
u$-integrable. { fseries($\Rightarrow$1.)} This follows from the hypothesis applying a more general Lemma for f divergences, see ProbabilityTheory.integrable\_f\_rnDeriv\_of\_integrable\_compProd' in the lean code. { fseries($\Rightarrow$3.)} i.\ implies that $\mu$-a.e.\ $y \mapsto  rac{d \kappa(x)}{d \eta(x)}(y) \log \left( rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x)  rac{d \kappa(x)}{d \eta(x)}(y) ight)$ is $\eta(x)$-integrable, hence $y \mapsto \log \left( rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x)  rac{d \kappa(x)}{d \eta(x)}(y) ight) = \log  rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x) + \log  rac{d \kappa(x)}{d \eta(x)}(y)$ is $\kappa(x)$-integrable. Then, since $\log  rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x)$ is constant in $y$ and $\kappa(x)$ is a finite measure, $y \mapsto \log  rac{d \kappa(x)}{d \eta(x)}(y)$ is $\kappa(x)$-integrable. { fseries($\Rightarrow$2.)} ii.\ implies that $x \mapsto \int_y  rac{d \kappa(x)}{d \eta(x)}(y) \log \left( rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x)  rac{d \kappa(x)}{d \eta(x)}(y) ight) \partial \eta (x) = \int_y \log \left( rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x)  rac{d \kappa(x)}{d \eta(x)}(y) ight) \partial \kappa (x)$ is $\mu$-integrable. Thanks to 3.\ we can split the integral: $$\int_y \log \left( rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x)  rac{d \kappa(x)}{d \eta(x)}(y) ight) \partial \kappa (x) = \int_y \log  rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x) \partial \kappa (x) + \int_y \log  rac{d \kappa(x)}{d \eta(x)}(y) \partial \kappa (x) = \log  rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x) + \int_y \log  rac{d \kappa(x)}{d \eta(x)}(y) \partial \kappa (x)$$ Then using 1.\ we can conclude that $x \mapsto \int_y \log  rac{d \kappa(x)}{d \eta(x)}(y) \partial \kappa (x)$ is $\mu$-integrable.

nodes.statement:
By Lemma~ef{lem:ac_compProd_iff}, $\mu \otimes \kappa \ll

u \otimes \eta$, $\mu \ll 
u$ and $\mu \otimes \kappa \ll \mu \otimes \eta$. TODO: deal with the non-integrable case, without using Lemma~ef{lem:integrable_llr_compProd_iff} that requires countably generated sigma-algebras. Suppose then that all three log-likelihood ratios are integrable. We use the chain rule for Radon-Nikodym derivatives (Theorem~ef{thm:rnDeriv_chain_compProd}).  egin{align*} \mathrm{KL}(\mu \otimes \kappa, 
u \otimes \eta) &= \int_p \log  rac{d(\mu \otimes \kappa)}{d(
u \otimes \eta)}(p) \partial (\mu \otimes \kappa) \ &= \int_x \int_y\log \left( rac{d\mu}{d 
u}(x) rac{d(\mu \otimes \kappa)}{d (\mu \otimes \eta)}(x,y)ight) \partial \kappa(x) \partial\mu \ &= \int_x \int_y\log \left( rac{d\mu}{d 
u}(x)ight) + \log \left( rac{d(\mu \otimes \kappa)}{d (\mu \otimes \eta)}(x,y)ight) \partial \kappa(x) \partial\mu \ &= \int_x \log \left( rac{d\mu}{d 
u}(x)ight)\partial\mu + \int_x \int_y\log \left( rac{d(\mu \otimes \kappa)}{d (\mu \otimes \eta)}(x,y)ight) \partial \kappa(x) \partial\mu \ &= \int_x \log \left( rac{d\mu}{d 
u}(x)ight)\partial\mu + \int_p\log \left( rac{d(\mu \otimes \kappa)}{d (\mu \otimes \eta)}(p)ight) \partial (\mu \otimes \kappa) \ &= \mathrm{KL}(\mu, 
u) + \mathrm{KL}(\mu \otimes \kappa, \mu \otimes \eta) \: . \end{align*}

u}(x) rac{d\kappa}{d \eta}(x,y)ight) \partial \kappa(x) \partial\mu \ &= \int_x \int_y\log \left( rac{d\mu}{d

nodes.statement: The main tool is Lemma~\ref{lem:fDiv_le_of_deriv2_le}. $\mathrm{JS}_\alpha$ is an $f$-divergence with function $f(x) = \alpha x \log(x) - (\alpha x + 1 - \alpha) \log (\alpha x + 1 - \alpha)$. On probability measures, $(1 - \lambda)\mathrm{H}_\lambda$ is an $f$-divergence with function $g(x) = 1 - x^\lambda + \lambda(x-1)$. These two functions satisfy $f(1) = 0$, $g(1) = 0$, $f'(1) = 0$, $g'(1) = 0$ and have second derivatives, hence Lemma~\ref{lem:fDiv_le_of_deriv2_le} applies and to obtain the inequality it suffices to compute $\sup_x\frac{f''(x)}{g''(x)}$~. \begin{align*} f''(x) &= \frac{\alpha(1 - \alpha)}{x(\alpha x + 1 - \alpha)} \: , \\ g''(x) &= \lambda (1 - \lambda) x^{\lambda - 2} \: . \end{align*} Let $h(x) = \frac{f''(x)}{g''(x)} = \frac{\alpha (1 - \alpha)}{\lambda (1 - \lambda)} \frac{x^{1 - \lambda}}{\alpha x + 1 - \alpha}$~. Its maximum is attained at a point where $h'(x) = 0$. \begin{align*} h'(x) = \frac{\alpha (1 - \alpha)}{\lambda (1 - \lambda)} \frac{(1 - \alpha)(1 - \lambda)x^{-\lambda} - \alpha \lambda x^{1 - \lambda}}{(\alpha x + 1 - \alpha)^2} \: . \end{align*} The optimum for $h$ is attained at $x = \frac{(1 - \alpha)(1 - \lambda)}{\alpha \lambda}$ and the maximal value of $h$ is $\frac{(1 - \alpha)^{1 - \lambda} \alpha^\lambda}{\lambda^{1 - \lambda} (1 - \lambda)^\lambda}$~.

nodes.name: Measurable space of measures
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal B$ be the Borel $\sigma$-algebra on $\mathbb{R}_{+,\infty}$. Let $\mathcal X$ be a measurable space. For a measurable set $s$ of $\mathcal X$, let $(\mu \mapsto \mu(s))^* \mathcal B$ be the $\sigma$-algebra on $\mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ defined by the comap of the evaluation function at $s$. Then $\mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ is a measurable space with $\sigma$-algebra $\bigsqcup_{s} (\mu \mapsto \mu(s))^* \mathcal B$ where the supremum is over all measurable sets $s$.
nodes.label: def:measure_measurableSpace

nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal X, \mathcal Y$ be measurable spaces, and let $f : \mathcal X \to \mathcal M(\mathcal Y)$ such that for all measurable sets $s$ of $\mathcal X$, the function $x \mapsto f(x)(s)$ is measurable. Then $f$ is measurable.
nodes.label: lem:measurable_measure_fun

nodes.name: Kernel
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal X, \mathcal Y$ be two measurable spaces. A probability transition kernel (or simply kernel) from $\mathcal X$ to $\mathcal Y$ is a measurable map from $\mathcal X$ to $\mathcal M (\mathcal Y)$, the measurable space of measures on $\mathcal Y$. We write $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ for a kernel $\kappa$ from $\mathcal X$ to $\mathcal Y$.
nodes.label: def:kernel

nodes.name: Deterministic kernel
nodes.statement: The deterministic kernel defined by a measurable function $f : \mathcal X \to \mathcal Y$ is the kernel $d_f: \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ defined by $d_f(x) = \delta_{f(x)}$, where for any $y \in \mathcal Y$, $\delta_y$ is the Dirac probability measure at $y$.
nodes.label: def:deterministic_kernel

nodes.statement: Two kernels $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ are equal iff for all measurable functions $f : \mathcal Y \to \mathbb{R}_{+,\infty}$ and all $x \in \mathcal X$, \begin{align*} \int_y f(y) \partial \kappa(x) = \int_y f(y) \partial \eta(x) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: thm:kernel_ext

nodes.name: Finite kernel
nodes.statement: A kernel $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ is said to be finite if there exists $C < +\infty$ such that for all $x \in \mathcal X$, $\kappa(x)(\mathcal Y) \le C$.
nodes.label: def:finite_kernel

nodes.name: Markov kernel
nodes.statement: A kernel $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ is said to be a Markov kernel if for all $x \in \mathcal X$, $\kappa(x)$ is a probability measure.
nodes.label: def:markov_kernel

nodes.name: s-finite kernel
nodes.statement: A kernel $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ is said to be a s-finite if it is equal to a countable sum of finite kernels.
nodes.label: def:sFinite_kernel

nodes.name: Composition-product
nodes.statement: Let $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ and $\eta : (\mathcal X \times \mathcal Y) \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z$ be two s-finite kernels. The composition-product of $\kappa$ and $\eta$ is a kernel $\kappa \otimes \eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow (\mathcal Y \times \mathcal Z)$ such that for all measurable functions $f : \mathcal Y \times \mathcal Z \to \mathbb{R}_{+,\infty}$ and $x \in \mathcal X$~, \begin{align*} \int_{y,z} f(y,z) \partial(\kappa \otimes \eta)(x) = \int_y \int_z f(y,z) \partial\eta(x,y) \partial\kappa(x) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: def:kernel_compProd

nodes.name: Composition-product of a measure and a kernel
nodes.statement: Let $\mu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ be an s-finite measure and $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be an s-finite kernel. Let $\mathcal U$ be a measurable space with a unique element $u$. Let $\mu_k : \mathcal U \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$ be the constant kernel with value $\mu$. The composition-product of $\mu$ and $\kappa$ is the measure on $\mathcal M(\mathcal X \times \mathcal Y)$ defined by $(\mu_k \otimes \kappa) (u)$~.
nodes.label: def:measure_compProd

nodes.name: Composition
nodes.statement: Let $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ and $\eta : \mathcal Y \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z$ be two kernels. The composition of $\kappa$ and $\eta$ is the kernel $\eta \circ \kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z$ such that for all measurable functions $f : \mathcal Z \to \mathbb{R}_{+,\infty}$ and all $x \in \mathcal X$, \begin{align*} \int_z f(z) \partial(\eta \circ \kappa)(x) = \int_y \int_z f(z) \partial\eta(y) \partial\kappa(x) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: def:kernel_comp

nodes.name: Product
nodes.statement: Let $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ and $\eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z$ be two s-finite kernels. The product of $\kappa$ and $\eta$ is the kernel $\kappa \times \eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y \times \mathcal Z$ such that for all measurable functions $f : \mathcal Y \times \mathcal Z \to \mathbb{R}_{+,\infty}$ and all $x \in \mathcal X$, \begin{align*} \int_{y,z} f(y,z) \partial(\kappa \times \eta)(x) = \int_y \int_z f(y,z) \partial\eta(x) \partial\kappa(x) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: def:kernel_prod

nodes.name: Parallel product
nodes.statement: Let $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ and $\eta : \mathcal X' \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y'$ be two s-finite kernels. The parallel product of $\kappa$ and $\eta$ is the kernel $\kappa \parallel \eta : \mathcal X \times \mathcal X' \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y \times \mathcal Y'$ such that for all measurable functions $f : \mathcal Y \times \mathcal Y' \to \mathbb{R}_{+,\infty}$ and all $x \in \mathcal X \times \mathcal X'$, \begin{align*} \int_{y,y'} f(y,y') \partial(\kappa \parallel \eta)(x,x') = \int_y \int_{y'} f(y,y') \partial\eta(x') \partial\kappa(x) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: def:kernel_parallel_prod

nodes.name: Blackwell sufficiency
nodes.statement: We define a partial order on kernels by the following. Let $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ and $\eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z$ (with same domain as $\kappa$). Then $\kappa$ is Blackwell sufficient for $\eta$, denoted by $\eta \le_B \kappa$, if there exists a Markov kernel $\xi : \mathcal Y \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z$ such that $\eta = \xi \circ \kappa$.
nodes.label: def:blackwellOrder

nodes.name: Disintegration in standard Borel spaces
nodes.statement: If either $\mathcal X$ is countable of $\mathcal Y$ has a countably generated $\sigma$-algebra, and $\mathcal Z$ is standard Borel, then for every s-finite kernel $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y \times \mathcal Z$, there exists a Markov kernel $\kappa_{Z \mid Y} : \mathcal X \times \mathcal Y \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z$ that disintegrates $\kappa$.
nodes.label: thm:disintegration

nodes.statement: Dummy node to summarize kernel properties.

nodes.statement: For $\mu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ and $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$, a Bayesian inverse of $\kappa$ is a Markov kernel $\kappa_\mu^\dagger : \mathcal Y \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$ such that $\mu \otimes \kappa = ((\kappa \circ \mu) \otimes \kappa_\mu^\dagger)_\leftrightarrow$ in which $(\cdot)_\leftrightarrow$ denotes swapping the two coordinates. If such an inverse exists it is unique up to a $(\kappa \circ \mu)$-null set, and we talk about \emph{the} Bayesian inverse of $\kappa$ with respect to $\mu$.
nodes.label: def:bayesInv

nodes.name: Existence of the Bayesian inverse
nodes.statement: For $\mathcal X$ standard Borel, $\mu$ and $\kappa$ s-finite, the Bayesian inverse of $\kappa$ with respect to $\mu$ exists and is obtained by disintegration of the measure $\mu \otimes \kappa$ on $\mathcal X \times \mathcal Y$ into a measure $\kappa \circ \mu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal Y)$ and a Markov kernel $\kappa_\mu^\dagger : \mathcal Y \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$.
nodes.label: lem:exists_bayesInv

nodes.name: a.e.-uniqueness of the Bayesian inverse
nodes.statement: Let $\mu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ be a finite measure and let $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be a finite kernel. If $\eta : \mathcal Y \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$ is such that $\mu \otimes \kappa = ((\kappa \circ \mu) \otimes \eta)_\leftrightarrow$, then $\eta(y) = \kappa_\mu^\dagger(y)$ for $(\kappa \circ \mu)$-almost all $y$.
nodes.label: lem:eq_bayesInv_of_compProd_eq

For $\mu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ s-finite, $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ a Markov kernel and $\kappa_\mu^\dagger$ the Bayesian inverse of $\kappa$ with respect to $\mu$, these objects satisfy the equality $\kappa_\mu^\dagger \circ \kappa \circ \mu = \mu$.
nodes.label: lem:bayesInv_comp_self

nodes.statement: The measure $\kappa_\mu^\dagger \circ (\kappa \circ \mu)$ is the projection on $\mathcal X$ of $(\kappa \circ \mu) \otimes \kappa_\mu^\dagger$. But $(\kappa \circ \mu) \otimes \kappa_\mu^\dagger = (\mu \otimes \kappa)_\leftrightarrow$ by definition of the Bayesian inverse. Since $\kappa$ is a Markov kernel, the projection on $\mathcal X$ of that measure is simply $\mu$.

For $\mathcal X$ and $\mathcal Y$ two standard Borel spaces, $\mu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ s-finite and $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ a Markov kernel, $(\kappa_\mu^\dagger)_{\kappa \circ \mu}^\dagger = \kappa$ ($\mu$-a.e.).
nodes.label: lem:bayesInv_self

nodes.statement: By uniqueness of the disintegration, it suffices to show that $(\kappa \circ \mu) \otimes \kappa_\mu^\dagger = ((\kappa_\mu^\dagger \circ \kappa \circ \mu) \otimes \kappa)_\leftrightarrow$~. By Lemma~\ref{lem:bayesInv_comp_self}, $\kappa_\mu^\dagger \circ \kappa \circ \mu = \mu$ and we need to prove $(\kappa \circ \mu) \otimes \kappa_\mu^\dagger = (\mu \otimes \kappa)_\leftrightarrow$~. This is true by definition of $\kappa_\mu^\dagger$~.
Let $\mu \in \mathcal M (\mathcal X)$ and let $\textup{id} : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$ be the identity kernel. Then $\textup{id}_\mu^\dagger = \textup{id}$.
nodes.label: lem:bayesInv_id

nodes.statement: It suffices to show that $\mu \otimes \textup{id} = ((\textup{id} \circ \mu) \otimes \textup{id})_\leftrightarrow$~, which is clear.

Let $\mu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$, $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ and $\eta : \mathcal Y \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z$. Then $(\eta \circ \kappa \circ \mu)$-a.e., \begin{align*} (\eta \circ \kappa)_\mu^\dagger = \kappa_{\mu}^\dagger \circ \eta_{\kappa \circ \mu}^\dagger \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:bayesInv_comp

nodes.statement: It suffices to show that $\mu \otimes (\eta \circ \kappa) = ((\eta \circ \kappa \circ \mu) \otimes (\kappa_{\mu}^\dagger \circ \eta_{\kappa \circ \mu}^\dagger))_\leftrightarrow$. TODO: transcribe the code.

Let $\mu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ and $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ such that $\kappa_\mu^\dagger$ exists and such that $\kappa(x) \ll \kappa \circ \mu$ almost surely. Then for $\mu$-almost all $x$ and $(\kappa \circ \mu)$-almost all $y$, \begin{align*} \frac{d \kappa_\mu^\dagger(y)}{d \mu}(x) = \frac{d \kappa(x)}{d(\kappa \circ \mu)}(y) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:rnDeriv_bayesInv

nodes.statement: $\mu$-almost all $x$ and $(\kappa \circ \mu)$-almost all $y$ is the same as $(\mu \times (\kappa \circ \mu))$-almost all $(x, y)$. It suffices to show that for all measurable sets of $\mathcal X \times \mathcal Y$, the integrals with respect to that product measure of the two sides of the equality on the set are equal. Furthermore, it is sufficient to show it for sets of the form $s \times t$ since those are a $\pi$-system. Since $\kappa(x) \ll \kappa \circ \mu$ almost surely, we have $\mu \otimes \kappa \ll \mu \times (\kappa \circ \mu)$, hence $(\kappa \circ \mu) \otimes \kappa_\mu^\dagger \ll (\kappa \circ \mu) \times \mu$. We get that $\kappa_\mu^\dagger(y) \ll \mu$ almost surely. \begin{align*} \int_{x \in s, y \in t} \frac{d \kappa_\mu^\dagger(y)}{d \mu}(x) \partial (\mu \times (\kappa \circ \mu)) &= \int_{y \in t} \int_{x \in s} \frac{d \kappa_\mu^\dagger(y)}{d \mu}(x) \partial \mu \partial (\kappa \circ \mu) \\ &= \int_{y \in t} \kappa_\mu^\dagger(y)(s) \partial (\kappa \circ \mu) \\ &= ((\kappa \circ \mu) \otimes \kappa_\mu^\dagger) (t \times s) \: . \end{align*} \begin{align*} \int_{x \in s, y \in t} \frac{d \kappa(x)}{d(\kappa \circ \mu)}(y) \partial (\mu \times (\kappa \circ \mu)) &= \int_{x \in s} \int_{y \in t} \frac{d \kappa(x)}{d(\kappa \circ \mu)}(y) \partial (\kappa \circ \mu) \partial \mu \\ &= \int_{x \in s} \kappa(x)(t) \partial \mu \\ &= (\mu \otimes \kappa) (s \times t) \: . \end{align*} By the defining property of the Bayesian inverse, those two quantities are equal.

The Radon-Nikodym derivative of $\kappa$ with respect to $\eta$, denoted by $\frac{d \kappa}{d \eta}$, is a measurable function $\mathcal X \times \mathcal Y \to \mathbb{R}_{+, \infty}$ with $\kappa = \frac{d \kappa}{d \eta} \cdot \eta + \kappa_{\perp \eta}$, where for all $x$, $\kappa_{\perp \eta}(x) \perp \eta(x)$.

Then for all $x \in \mathcal X$, $\kappa(x) = f(x, \cdot) \cdot \eta(x) + \xi(x)$ with $\xi(x) \perp \eta(x)$. By the uniqueness result for the Radon-Nikodym derivative of measures, $f(x, \cdot) = \frac{d \kappa(x)}{d \eta(x)}$ almost everywhere.

Let $\mu, 
u$ be two finite measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X ightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be two finite kernels, with either $\mathcal X$ countable or $\mathcal{Y}$ countably generated. Then for $(
u \otimes \eta)$-almost all $(x, y)$,  egin{align*}  rac{d (\mu \otimes \kappa)}{d (
u \otimes \eta)}(x,y) =  rac{d\mu}{d
u}(x) rac{d \kappa}{d \eta}(x,y) \: . \end{align*} This implies that the equality is true for $
u$-almost all $x$, for $\eta(x)$-almost all $y$.

nodes.statement:
First, by Theorem~ef{thm:rnDeriv_chain_compProd}, for $(
u \otimes \eta)$-almost all $(x,y)$,  egin{align*}  rac{d(\mu \otimes \kappa)}{d(
u \otimes \eta)}(x, y) =  rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x)  rac{d(\mu \otimes \kappa)}{d(\mu \otimes \eta)}(x, y) \: . \end{align*} It remains to show that $ rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x)  rac{d(\mu \otimes \kappa)}{d(\mu \otimes \eta)}(x, y)$ is $(
u \otimes \eta)$-almost everywhere equal to $ rac{d\mu}{d
u}(x) rac{d \kappa}{d \eta}(x,y)$. By Lemma~ef{cor:rnDeriv_compProd_right}, $(\mu \otimes \eta)$-almost surely,  egin{align*}  rac{d \kappa}{d \eta} =  rac{d (\mu \otimes \kappa)}{d (\mu \otimes \eta)} \: . \end{align*} We then use Lemma~ef{lem:ae_rnDeriv_ne_zero} to turn that into a $(
u \otimes \eta)$-almost sure equality:  egin{align*}  rac{d(\mu \otimes \eta)}{d(
u \otimes \eta)} rac{d \kappa}{d \eta} =  rac{d(\mu \otimes \eta)}{d(
u \otimes \eta)} rac{d (\mu \otimes \kappa)}{d (\mu \otimes \eta)} \: . \end{align*} Finally, by Lemma~ef{cor:rnDeriv_compProd_left}, $ rac{d(\mu \otimes \eta)}{d(
u \otimes \eta)} =  rac{d\mu}{d
u}$ almost surely.
